# Introduction

Can changes in population-level dietary trends track with downstream changes in population-level health outcomes? 

Specifically, can a population's increase in a relatively plant-based dietary pattern be correlated with a time-lagged decrease in that population's elevated LDL cholesterol risk level? If so, at how long a time lag? 

This study examines the population of the United Kingdom (UK), drawing on diet diary data from a representative sample of nearly 190,000 UK households from 1974 to 2000, and population-level chronic disease risk factor rates (especially high LDL cholesterol) from 1990 to 2023. 

Diet diary data is assessed by both food group profile and nutrient profile. Each household's reported food acquisition is aggregated and normalized against that household's total calories, painting a quantity-agnostic picture of that household's diet composition. A machine-learning pipeline is then applied to the household level data, with a cross-validated stability optimized k-means clustering algorithm designating a cluster identity for each household, and with principal component analysis (PCA) being used to orient and explain the findings.  

The year-on-year changes to the population-level proportion of households assigned to any of these k-means clusters over time serves as the explanatory variable for the correlative analysis against downstream population level LDL cholesterol risk rates.

Ultimately, this study identifies a statistically significant inverse correlation between population-level year-on-year changes in relatively-plant-based diet patterns and risk of high LDL cholesterol, at a five-year-time lag.
